title: Opening Remarks
description: AI engineering meets Wall Street: a room of builders comparing what already works, and what might become normal next.

title: Vault: Making Unstructured Data Work for Investing

speakers.name: Sam Green
speakers.role: Team Lead, Applied AI - AIA Labs

description: Investment agents need the research an investor would read—and a way to remember what the firm learns. Bridgewater’s Vault puts both into the same research loop.

title: Balancing Acceleration and Safety for AI Agents
description: John Feminella uses a catastrophic payment mistake to explain five controls that make agents visible, constrain their access, and reserve human attention for decisions that need it.

title: Does Code Quality Even Matter?
description: Cheap code makes some programs disposable. For the systems people will keep changing, Max Kanat-Alexander argues that AI should make engineering rigor cheaper too.

title: What does an AI engineer do?
description: Arize Signal reads traces, finds recurring problems, and can propose fixes. Building that loop requires decisions about memory, temporary access, recovery, and what counts as a good fix.

title: Wells Fargo Foundation Model: Application to Fraud Detection at Scale

speakers.name: Freddy Lecue
speakers.role: Head of Frontier AI Models, Managing Director

description: Freddy Lecue explains why Wells Fargo trained a transformer on transactions rather than text, how it tokenizes heterogeneous banking data, and how the resulting representation supports fraud detection.

title: Inside Arca’s long-horizon agents that run the business
description: Aman Singh follows one client’s tax payment across days of analysis, approval, trading, and settlement to show how Arca’s agents keep work moving between human decisions.

title: Intent Based Auth
description: Permission to call a payment API cannot tell an agent whether it should pay this invoice again. This panel explores how mission history, budgets, and changing conditions can inform each authorization decision.

title: We Let Our Financial Planners Write the Agents
description: At Range, financial planners write and maintain the skills that draft their work. Matt Ragone explains how to turn professional judgment into a repeatable process without handing client communication to an agent.

title: Your Agent Is a Lethal Trifecta (and What to Do About It)
description: An on-call agent can be useful and dangerously overprivileged at the same time. Kim Maida follows the same incident queue before and after adding identity, token exchange, and task-scoped policy.

title: Your GPU Neighbor Can Hear Your Model
description: Branislav Brzak demonstrates how timing on shared GPUs can reveal model behavior even when memory and compute are partitioned, then explains what operators can control.

title: Please… Enough with the Sloppy, One-Shot SaaS Replacements
description: A working internal app can still be unpleasant to use. Mahmoud Abdelwahab walks through the product details, reusable patterns, and verification loop behind Railway’s agent-built marketing tools.

title: Just-in-Time Ontologies
description: The meaning of a customer depends on the decision being made. Hrishi Olickel explains why data pipelines need contextual schemas, distinct model roles, and bounded experiments that can trade cost against quality.

title: Building Reliable, yet Smart Workflows for Finance, Wealth and Insurance
description: A request to complete one form can become a process lasting days. Karthic Rao follows that request through Perpetual’s compiler, approval gates, and typed model calls.

title: Agents in Orbit: Workflows, Not Autopilot
description: Flywire’s Orbit brings engineering agents into an existing GitLab and AWS environment. This opening excerpt covers the company’s infrastructure and privacy constraints before the livestream returns to the live stage.
coverage: Interrupted livestream excerpt (2 minutes). The reading edition links the complete recording.

title: Great Agents Start with Great Infrastructure
description: A spreadsheet with an agent behind every cell needs fast compute, shared storage, and deliberate isolation. Akshat Bubna explains how those requirements change the sandbox beneath an agent.

title: Beyond the Model Card: The Jagged Frontier of AI in Finance
description: A model can earn strong partial credit and still produce work that cannot be sent to a client. Rayan Krishnan shows how evaluations built from a firm’s own work can guide model choice, spending, and deployment.

title: AI and the Future of Fundamental Investing
description: Jack Woodruff sees AI changing research preparation and analysts’ roles while leaving a central investment problem intact: deciding where limited human attention can uncover a divergent view.

title: Shipping like a startup, regulated like a bank
description: David Abitbol describes Revolut’s move toward self-hosted coding models, the inference tuning that made them practical, and the operational controls used around a regulated engineering organization.

title: Everyone Has AI. Who Has the Advantage?

speakers.name: Sid Pednekar
speakers.role: Head of Data and AI | Asset Management

description: Sid Pednekar follows two hypothetical investment firms to show why widespread access to AI can still produce very different results: the scarce resource is the judgment that shapes the work.

title: Welcome Back - Featured Keynotes
description: Alex Lieberman returns to the adoption gap: distributing an LLM is much more common than putting agents to work across a business.

title: A Hedge Fund as a Function
description: Frank Long models an investment firm as a function that turns external and internal context into selection, size, and timing. The engineering challenge appears when that function is decomposed into work that code, models, and people can each perform well.

title: Frontier Models for Acting in Space and Time
description: Pim de Witte explains General Intuition’s bet on action-labeled game data: models that observe continuously and select actions while the world keeps moving, with language models available for longer-term planning.

title: Hermes gives you wings: Build on open foundations.
description: Dillon Rolnick makes the case for owning the agent layer as AI becomes part of everyday business operations. His argument connects model economics to a practical architecture: interchangeable models beneath software and workflows a company controls.

title: Closing Remarks
description: The closing invitation is simple: turn the day’s ideas into conversations with the people who are building them.

title: Welcome Remarks
description: Ksenia Se opens the final day of AI Engineer NYC with a question about how agent capabilities change the work inside companies.

title: Chasing capabilities while waiting for the frontier

speakers.name: Alexander Shevchenko
speakers.role: Head of Ramp Labs and Applied Research

description: Ramp keeps adopting better frontier models. Alexander Shevchenko shows where specialist training, prepared context, and parallel agents can still save users time before the next model arrives.

title: The Machine that Changed the World, vAI
description: Agents can produce code much faster than a company can ship it. Tariq Shaukat uses factory design to explain where guidance, independent verification, and evidence belong in an agentic development process.

title: Trusting Agents in Policy-Driven Workflows
description: A regulated workflow can move forward through fixed approval stages while agents iterate inside each stage. Evan Kormos explains how to choose those stages, evaluate the work, and reduce supervision only when measured confidence supports it.

title: Building the Next Chapter of AI in Finance

speakers.name: Joseph Kim
speakers.role: Head of ChatGPT for Financial Services

description: A capable model still needs financial data, familiar outputs, and a way to check its work. Joseph Kim explains the product choices behind ChatGPT for Financial Services and the thresholds he expects finance agents to cross next.

title: Security in the Age of AI: Recent Attacks, Incidents & Defenses

speakers.name: Andrey Rybka
speakers.role: Head of Architecture & Emerging Technologies in the Office of the CTO

description: Andrey Rybka follows failures from stolen credentials to poisoned memory. His defense starts with what an agent can actually do: short-lived identities, checks outside the model, and limits that stop execution.

title: Towards Autonomous Analysts in Finance
description: An investment team needs more than a chatbot that produces a spreadsheet. Yijia Liang explains why Compound built shared agents, its own Office engines, and tools for navigating large data rooms before asking analysts to delegate longer pieces of work.

title: Not All GPU's Are Deployed The Same
description: Two deployments of the same GPU can produce different amounts of useful output. Oliver Kennon separates chip rental prices from production costs, then explains why operators, service definitions, and benchmarks matter to the compute market.

title: How Compute Markets Work
description: Evan Conrad traces compute markets back to a startup’s inability to buy the right amount of reliable capacity—and explains why his company ended up operating both the exchange and the hardware.

title: The Dark Pools of Compute
description: Affaan Mustafa and Alejandro Soumah Fernandez map the financing, delivery, and price risks hidden inside a GPU-hour quote—and the market structures needed to separate them.

title: Compute Exchange
description: Carmen Li demonstrates a neutral market for reserved GPUs, forward contracts, and used hardware, then connects procurement terms to forward curves and residual asset value.

title: Paving the Road to Production: Governed Enterprise AI Agents
description: Harish Gaggar follows an enterprise agent from registration and deployment through authenticated tool calls, checkpoints, evaluation records, privacy controls, and context optimization.

title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It?
description: Michele Grant follows an acquisition-reporting agent from a successful pilot to the evidence, ownership, and review practices needed for greater autonomy.

title: Tokens Are the Cheap Part
description: A rising AI bill can accompany a falling cost of delivery. Steve Jamison combines salary and token spending to examine the cost of a merged pull request—and checks whether the apparent gains hide smaller changes or worse quality.

title: The Automated Security Master: keeping your master database clean with agents
description: In this livestream excerpt, Amol Kapoor and Clifford Ressel explain how cloud agents can trace a changed security-master cell back to its evidence—and why the person who understands the discrepancy still matters.
coverage: Interrupted livestream excerpt; the recording cuts off during the discussion.

title: Built to Scale: Future-Proofing Your Technology Roadmap
description: John Stecher and Scott Worland explain where to invest as models improve: accessible data, evaluations, and production controls—and where to stay willing to replace yesterday’s code.

title: Why Wall Street Still Doesn’t Trust AI
description: Vinoo Ganesh separates numerical trust into source selection, exact retrieval, arithmetic, access control, and output verification—and explains why a citation added at the end cannot do all those jobs.

title: Coding an Autonomous Wall Street Coworker: Custom Skills, Connectors, and Event Hooks
description: A useful background agent needs a workspace, a playbook, credentials, and rules for when to act. Philipp Schmid builds a portfolio-auditing coworker around Gemini Managed Agents, showing how those pieces fit together.

title: Your Company Has No Model of Itself: Bootstrapping a World Model from Slack, Decks and Meetings
description: A green status slide can conceal a project already slipping. Joao Wenzel describes a system that tracks what a company believes, how old the evidence is, and what happens next—then asks people to correct the beliefs that matter.

title: Self-Improving Organizations
description: Will Brown describes how an organization’s corrections, decisions, and repeated workflows could become training data. Start with evaluations and routing, then give specialized models a way to improve alongside the people using them.

title: The Cost of Accessibility in AI
description: Jemima Abu uses a small coding-agent experiment to show how missing accessibility requirements create extra code, extra repair work, and products people cannot use.

title: Your AI Isn’t the Problem. Your Infrastructure Is.
description: This livestream excerpt captures Jiachen Jiang’s opening argument: an instruction to avoid destructive work is weaker than infrastructure that prevents the action.
coverage: Opening excerpt only; the recording cuts off before the incident case studies. The reading edition links the complete recording.

title: Welcome Back — Featured Keynotes
description: Ksenia Se returns for the final keynotes with a practical conference project: use an agent to research potential employers, then make the introductions yourself.

title: AI in Practice: An Inside Look at Apollo's Approach

speakers.name: Jack McDonald
speakers.role: Principal at Apollo Global Management, COO of Redding Ridge

description: Michael Manapat and Jack McDonald explain how agents turn fragmented credit data into usable workflows: prepare a portfolio, reconcile financing activity, and leave investment judgment with the people responsible for it.

title: Process Supervision for Agents That Do Long-Horizon Work
description: Mitchell Troyanovsky shows how behavior specs, trajectory forks, and inexpensive simulations help diagnose agents that work for hours. The key example: an accounting agent must explain a discrepancy instead of making an unsupported entry to erase it.

title: Everything will be Simulated
description: Runway’s early films generated images to watch. Cristóbal Valenzuela shows research aimed at generating images people and agents can act on, moving from video clips toward interactive interfaces and shared visual reasoning.

title: Closing Remarks
description: Ksenia Se and swyx close the conference by returning to the conversations, engineering work, and community that continue after the talks.
